steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our short paper giving two counterexamples to the Rényi efficiency hypothesis from "Tokenization and the Noiseless Channel". Explain why intrinsic tokenizer evaluation is wanted, what that paper proposed, what our counterexamples show, and give the structure of the paper.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Tokenizer choice matters; need for intrinsic evaluation
2. Rényi efficiency proposal in Tokenization and the Noiseless Channel
3. Our counterexamples and what we hope they achieve
4. Structure

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Motivation
- tokenizer choice strongly impacts downstream NLP model performance
- hard to pick best: comparing needs fully training a model per tokenizer; days/weeks of compute
- -> intrinsic evaluation: easy-to-compute metrics from tokenized text only, signal downstream quality (Figure 1)

2. Rényi efficiency
- Tokenization and the Noiseless Channel: metric based on generalization of Shannon Entropy = Rényi efficiency of unigram distribution
- slightly better correlated with downstream performance (BLEU on translation) than percentile frequency metric (adopted from earlier work)
- much better correlated than Shannon Entropy and average sequence length
- good tokenizers: few rare tokens, but also not many very high-frequency tokens
- authors note it does not fully account for relative performance; other metrics left as open problem -> variance Rényi efficiency does not capture

3. This work
- two variants of BPE tokenizers: increase Rényi efficiency while degrading downstream performance
- contradicts hypothesis high Rényi efficiency -> better expected performance
- hope: spur research on where Rényi efficiency and related metrics predict performance and where they fail
- goal: better predictor of downstream performance from tokenized text

4. Structure
- 2) Byte-Pair Encoding; 3) Rényi efficiency, other metrics, hypotheses; 4) two families of counterexamples + proofs; 5) empirical verification with machine translation

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
The choice of tokenizer has a strong impact on the performance of the downstream NLP model. But it is also difficult to pick the best one, because comparing two tokenizers usually means fully training a model on top of each of them, and this can be prohibitively expensive, taking days or weeks of compute time. This is why people search for an intrinsic evaluation of tokenizers, that is, metrics that are easy to compute, that can be evaluated using only the tokenized text, and that signal whether the tokenization will be good for the downstream task (see Figure 1).

In Tokenization and the Noiseless Channel, the authors propose a new metric based on a generalization of Shannon Entropy, the Rényi efficiency of the unigram distribution. This quantity has a slightly better correlation with downstream model performance (BLEU score on a translation task) than a percentile frequency metric, which they adopted based on earlier work. Its correlation is also much better than Shannon Entropy and average sequence length. The authors suggest a characteristic of good tokenizers: a tokenizer should contain few rare tokens (tokens that appear infrequently in tokenized texts), but it should also not contain many very high-frequency tokens. They propose this metric for evaluating tokenizers intrinsically before training, but they note that it does not fully account for the relative performances of tokenizers, and they leave the search for other metrics as an open problem. This means there is some variance in the performances of all possible tokenizers that Rényi efficiency does not capture.

This work
- two BPE tokenizer variants: Rényi efficiency up, downstream performance down
- contradicts hypothesis: high Rényi efficiency -> better expected performance
- hope to spur research on where Rényi efficiency and related metrics work and fail; better predictor of downstream performance

Structure
- 2) Byte-Pair Encoding; 3) Rényi efficiency, other metrics, hypotheses; 4) two families of counterexamples + proofs; 5) empirical verification with machine translation

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
The choice of tokenizer has a strong impact on the performance of the downstream NLP model. But it is also difficult to pick the best one, because comparing two tokenizers usually means fully training a model on top of each of them, and this can be prohibitively expensive, taking days or weeks of compute time. This is why people search for an intrinsic evaluation of tokenizers, that is, metrics that are easy to compute, that can be evaluated using only the tokenized text, and that signal whether the tokenization will be good for the downstream task (see Figure 1).

In Tokenization and the Noiseless Channel, the authors propose a new metric based on a generalization of Shannon Entropy, the Rényi efficiency of the unigram distribution. This quantity has a slightly better correlation with downstream model performance (BLEU score on a translation task) than a percentile frequency metric, which they adopted based on earlier work. Its correlation is also much better than Shannon Entropy and average sequence length. The authors suggest a characteristic of good tokenizers: a tokenizer should contain few rare tokens (tokens that appear infrequently in tokenized texts), but it should also not contain many very high-frequency tokens. They propose this metric for evaluating tokenizers intrinsically before training, but they note that it does not fully account for the relative performances of tokenizers, and they leave the search for other metrics as an open problem. This means there is some variance in the performances of all possible tokenizers that Rényi efficiency does not capture.

In this work we introduce two variants of BPE tokenizers where we can explicitly increase Rényi efficiency while the downstream model performance gets worse. This goes against the hypothesis above that high Rényi efficiency implies better expected performance. We hope that these examples will help spur more research into where Rényi efficiency and other related metrics predict performance accurately and where they fail. In the end, these efforts are meant to create a better predictor of downstream performance for NLP tasks based on the tokenized text.

Structure:

- 2) Introduction to Byte-Pair Encoding.

- 3) Rényi efficiency, other metrics and their tokenization hypotheses.

- 4) Two families of counterexamples to the Rényi efficiency tokenization hypothesis, with proofs.

- 5) Empirical verification of the counterexamples with machine translation performance.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The tokenizer choice strongly impacts downstream NLP model performance [1]. At the same time, it is difficult to select the best one, because comparing two tokenizers typically requires fully training a model on top of each tokenizer, which can be prohibitively expensive, taking days or weeks of compute time. This motivates the search for an intrinsic evaluation of tokenizers — easy-to-compute metrics that can be evaluated using only the tokenized text and that signal whether the tokenization will be good for the downstream task (see Figure 1).

In Tokenization and the Noiseless Channel, [2] propose a new metric based on a generalization of Shannon Entropy — the Rényi efficiency of the unigram distribution. This quantity is slightly better correlated with downstream model performance (BLEU score on a translation task) than a percentile frequency metric, which they adopted based on [3]. It is also much better correlated than Shannon Entropy [4] and average sequence length. The authors suggest a characteristic of good tokenizers: not only should a tokenizer contain few rare tokens (tokens that appear infrequently in tokenized texts), it should also not contain many very high-frequency tokens. While they propose this metric for evaluating tokenizers intrinsically before training, they note that it does not fully account for the relative performances of tokenizers and leave the search for other metrics as an open problem. In other words, there is some variance in the performances of all possible tokenizers that Rényi efficiency does not capture.

In this work, we introduce two variants of BPE tokenizers for which we can explicitly increase Rényi efficiency while degrading downstream model performance. This contradicts the aforementioned hypothesis that high Rényi efficiency implies better expected performance. We hope these examples will spur more research into where Rényi efficiency and related metrics accurately predict performance and where they fail. Ultimately, these efforts aim to create a better predictor of downstream performance for NLP tasks based on the tokenized text.

Structure:

- 2) Introduction to Byte-Pair Encoding.

- 3) Rényi efficiency, other metrics and their tokenization hypotheses.

- 4) Two families of counterexamples to the Rényi efficiency tokenization hypothesis, and proofs.

- 5) Empirical verification of the counterexamples with machine translation performance.
